claim_text: 來源機構：Journal of General Education and Humanities；資料標題：Tangible AI in the Elementary Classroom: Effects on AI Literacy, Computational Thinking, and Learner Dispositions；來源刊登日：2026-11-01。作者摘要報告：研究檢視實體 AI（tangible AI）介入後，學生運算思維、AI 概念掌握、學習動機與程式自我效能的變化，並探討教師的實施經驗；以整合 AI 素養框架與 SEAME 模型的架構設計四週（4 × 60 分鐘）介入，對象為一所公立小學五年級學生 36 人與教師 1 人，採混合方法中的單組前後測設計；作者寫明沒有對照組，變化無法歸於介入，單校結果屬初步。（AI 輔助摘要，未經真人逐則審稿；請參閱原文。）

original_excerpt: This study examined changes in computational thinking (CT), AI concept mastery, learning motivation, and programming self-efficacy following a tangible AI intervention, and explored the teacher's implementation experience. … Guided by a framework integrating the AI Literacy Framework and the SEAME Model, a four-week intervention (4 × 60 minutes) was implemented with 36 fifth-grade students and one teacher in a public elementary school, using a single-group pretest–posttest design within a mixed-methods approach. … Quantitative data were analyzed using repeated-measures ANCOVA, with prior computing experience as a covariate; qualitative data from semi-structured teacher interviews (during and after the intervention) and observations of all four sessions were analyzed thematically. … Tangible AI may offer a promising bridge to early AI literacy; however, without a control group, changes cannot be causally attributed to the intervention, and these single-school findings are preliminary.

summary_evidence_spans: This study examined changes in computational thinking (CT), AI concept mastery, learning motivation, and programming self-efficacy following a tangible AI intervention, and explored the teacher's implementation experience.

Guided by a framework integrating the AI Literacy Framework and the SEAME Model, a four-week intervention (4 × 60 minutes) was implemented with 36 fifth-grade students and one teacher in a public elementary school, using a single-group pretest–posttest design within a mixed-methods approach.

Quantitative data were analyzed using repeated-measures ANCOVA, with prior computing experience as a covariate; qualitative data from semi-structured teacher interviews (during and after the intervention) and observations of all four sessions were analyzed thematically.

Tangible AI may offer a promising bridge to early AI literacy; however, without a control group, changes cannot be causally attributed to the intervention, and these single-school findings are preliminary.
